title: The Adventure of the Speckled Band

teacherSummary.text: Helen Stoner fears for her life: her twin sister Julia died two years before, crying 'It was the band! The speckled band!' Now her violent stepfather, Dr. Grimesby Roylott, has moved her into Julia's room. Holmes and Watson notice a dummy bell-rope, a ventilator and a bed bolted to the floor. They wait in the dark; Holmes strikes at a swamp adder sent through the ventilator. The snake turns and kills Roylott, who had wanted the girls' inheritance.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “The Adventure of the Speckled Band,” how does Doyle show reason defeating a hidden crime? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In The Adventure of the Speckled Band, how does Doyle develop the idea of reason defeating a hidden crime? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the foreshadowing in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The Adventure of the Speckled Band develops the idea of reason defeating a hidden crime. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of foreshadowing and point of view shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of The Adventure of the Speckled Band (where it begins, turns and ends) and its foreshadowing shape the reader's understanding of reason defeating a hidden crime. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what The Adventure of the Speckled Band suggests about reason defeating a hidden crime. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's foreshadowing and point of view), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Arthur Conan Doyle uses foreshadowing in The Adventure of the Speckled Band to complicate the reader's understanding of reason defeating a hidden crime. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Adventure of the Speckled Band within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of reason defeating a hidden crime responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read The Adventure of the Speckled Band alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of reason defeating a hidden crime follows or bends those conventions, using the foreshadowing as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to The Adventure of the Speckled Band and its treatment of reason defeating a hidden crime. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's foreshadowing and point of view, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads The Adventure of the Speckled Band as evidence for a larger claim about reason defeating a hidden crime in The Adventure of the Speckled Band. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Adventure of the Speckled Band as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of reason defeating a hidden crime. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Adventure of the Speckled Band.

satQuestions.passage: "It is easy for me to be so, for every event of that dreadful time is seared into my memory. The manor-house is, as I have already said, very old, and only one wing is now inhabited. The bedrooms in this wing are on the ground floor, the sitting-rooms being in the central block of the buildings. Of these bedrooms the first is Dr. Roylott's, the second my sister's, and the third my own. There is no communication between them, but they all open out into the same corridor. Do I make myself plain?"

Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Sensitive content: Murder; domestic abuse implied. Preview the story, tell students in advance, and allow a pass on reading aloud. Keep discussion on how the writer uses these elements, not on graphic detail.
contentNotes.studentPreview: Heads-up: this story includes murder; domestic abuse implied.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “Why does the writer include this, and what does it make us notice?”
